Built on frozen DINOv2 patch features, SEAT couples mask-guided sign-specific attention for localized morphology, a semi-relaxed optimal transport pathway over LAB/HSV color prototypes to enhance pale-tongue recognition, and a co-occurrence-aware transport regularizer to shape the batch-level predicted label marginal. These components are evaluated through audits matched to their evidence types. On the TongueDx benchmark, SEAT achieves a mean macro-F1 of 72.59 with a standard deviation of 1.04 across six random seeds, with a six-model ensemble reaching 74.15. The ensemble outperforms a backbone-matched baseline and a larger, domain-specialized vision-language model by 8.06 and 2.99 percentage points, respectively. Our results demonstrate that aligning dedicated prediction pathways and audits with sign-specific characteristics improves multi-label accuracy while offering more targeted evidential grounding than uniform post-hoc spatial explanations. title_en: TIVS: Mapping the Sensitivity Landscape of Visual Token Transformations in MLLMs
abstract_en: Recent efforts to improve the efficiency of multimodal large language models (MLLMs) have explored visual token pruning, quantization, and feature compression. title_en: Joint Learning of Factual and Counterfactual Worlds for Causal Prior-data Fitted Networks
abstract_en: Estimating treatment effects is central to science across many disciplines and requires counterfactual reasoning about alternative worlds. In the real world, however, each unit reveals its outcome only under the factual world. Thus, the factual and counterfactual outcomes can never be jointly learned by any model trained on real data. The problem is therefore tractable only in synthetic settings, where both worlds can be generated. Recent progress on prior-data fitted networks (PFNs) has shown that models pre-trained purely on synthetic data can transfer to real-world prediction. This paradigm has since carried over to causal effect estimation. Despite this fully synthetic setup, existing causal PFNs carry the real-world constraint into their training objective, confining learning to a single world's outcome per unit. The dependence between the two worlds is thereby lost, and the density of the treatment effect relies by default on independence, which is implausible in practice. We therefore propose joint learning, a training setup in which a causal PFN learns the joint distribution of the factual and counterfactual outcomes of each unit. From the joint distribution, we obtain both the response and the individual treatment effect densities, and at inference, we apply optimal transport across units to obtain an approximation of the average treatment effect density. Ours is therefore the first causal PFN approach to provide all three densities together while accounting for the cross-world dependence. We apply joint learning and optimal transport to existing causal PFNs and evaluate it across semi-synthetic, synthetic, and real benchmarks spanning diverse causal scenarios. The jointly trained models significantly improve upon their baselines in point estimation and uncertainty quantification in most settings, indicating that joint learning is a preferable training setup for causal PFNs.

title_en: Sample-Efficient Ensemble Reinforcement Learning at Scale
abstract_en: Ensemble methods such as MeanQ have been shown to improve the sample efficiency of relatively small model-free deep reinforcement learning (RL) architectures, including DQN and similarly sized variants such as Rainbow. However, to our knowledge, the effects of ensembling on large-scale architectures such as Bigger Better Faster (BBF) have not been studied. In this work, we present MeanQ-BBF, a hybrid model-free algorithm that combines the principles of MeanQ and BBF. Through statistically rigorous evaluation on the Atari 100K benchmark, we show that in contrast to naive scaling of the network size of BBF, which degrades performance, MeanQ-BBF is able to leverage the increase in model capacity to improve performance over BBF. Moreover, MeanQ-BBF does this in a computationally efficient way by organizing the added parameters into largely independent learners. Finally, we discuss the performance-cost tradeoff in the context of practical sample-efficient RL.

title_en: Multiaccuracy as an Error Benchmark for Learning with Distribution Shift
abstract_en: Agnostic learning has a well-developed theory of computational and statistical complexity. For learning with distribution shift, even the choice of an appropriate error benchmark remains challenging. Testable learning with distribution shift (TDS) was introduced to develop computational foundations for this setting: using labeled training data and unlabeled test data, the learner must either produce a predictor with low test error or detect distribution shift. However, standard agnostic TDS guarantees allow a constant-factor amplification of the optimum error even when the training and test distributions coincide. They therefore do not directly recover the guarantee of classical agnostic learning. We introduce shift multiaccuracy, a stronger error benchmark inspired by multiaccuracy from algorithmic fairness. This yields a TDS formulation that becomes equivalent to multiaccuracy when there is no shift. Using a recent nontrivial reduction from agnostic learning to multiaccurate prediction from prior work, we obtain the first TDS framework that formally generalizes agnostic learning through an efficient reduction preserving the training marginal. The framework retains existing algorithmic upper bounds and inherits computational lower bounds from agnostic learning. Moreover, we establish a direct connection between our model and identity testing, yielding the first statistical characterization of agnostic TDS learning, in terms of Rademacher complexity. More broadly, we argue that shift multiaccuracy might be of independent interest in unsupervised domain adaptation, as it leads to sharper out-of-distribution generalization guarantees, and can be minimized directly, since its definition does not involve the unobserved test labels.

title_en: From Cloud to Edge: A Fully Local Pipeline for Pothole Risk Assessment and Driver Warning Generation
abstract_en: Vision-language models can turn road images into clear, geometry-aware pothole warnings, but current systems depend on commercial cloud services. They reach Cohen's kappa = 0.268 against human consensus at 28 ms per pothole, close to the cloud model's 0.321, within the camera setup they were trained for. A local 8-billion-parameter vision-language model writes the warnings under a grammar that admits only in-lane maneuvers. Three blind, independent raters scored these warnings safer than the cloud warnings (4.18 vs. 3.65 of 5; p = 0.001; 50 scenes) and equally clear, whereas an automated LLM judge ranked them the other way. title_en: Where Should LLM Agents Adapt at Test Time? In Context, in Weights, or Both
abstract_en: LLM agents operating repeatedly in the same environment, such as a code repository, a database, or an application suite, encounter tasks that share latent structure. Experience can reveal this structure, allowing agents to reuse environment knowledge and learn from environmental feedback. Agents can adapt at test-time using this experience through two channels: retaining it in context and updating their weights. These channels are usually studied separately, leaving unclear what each contributes and when they complement each other. We compare in-context learning (ICL), reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards using GRPO, and self-distillation using SDPO, alone and in combination, using a shared online protocol and modular framework. Agents encounter matched task streams, are evaluated on each task before adapting to it, and learn only from their own attempts and environment feedback. We evaluate 14 adaptation mechanisms and a stateless baseline with Qwen3.5-9B on 109 tasks from four environments drawn from SWE-bench Verified, AppWorld, ScienceWorld, and BIRD-Critic-SQLite, using five task orders per environment. ICL provides the largest standalone gain: its best policy raises mean success across environments from 28.8% to 49.4%. Adding GRPO to this policy achieves the highest mean success, 51.6%. While adding GRPO improves the overall mean under every ICL policy, SDPO has mixed effects. Trace analyses show fewer lookups and shorter attempts under ICL, consistent with reusing knowledge of the shared structure. However, ICL also frequently skips inspection and verification for the current task. Adding GRPO to ICL helps restore these behaviors while preserving its reduced environment lookups. These observations suggest that reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards can refine how agents use retained experience, motivating the joint study of context management and weight updates.

title_en: Data Attribution Should Steer Pretraining
abstract_en: Pretraining data curation decides what a model learns from, yet what makes a document worth learning from depends on what the model already knows. title_en: Attacker Diversity Reduction in Adaptive LLM Red Teaming
abstract_en: Reinforcement learning can make automated red-teaming more successful while narrowing the attacks it produces. Attack Diversity Retention (ADR) compares the within-behavior of the trained attacker spread with the untrained attacker. In order for an attack diversity to be consider as having been reduced, a criterion requires the ADR to be below a 0.75 target with a 95% confidence interval together with continued attacker effectiveness. Therefore, if an attacker narrows its attack vector by 25% consistently its considered less diverse. After 24 attacker and 12 defender LORA-based updates, ADR for the three runs were 0.63, 0.61 and 0.63, respectively. title_en: SG-LegalClarify: A Large-Scale Benchmark for Legal Reasoning and Ambiguity Recognition in Singapore Law
abstract_en: Singapore offers a distinctive testbed for legal reasoning by large language models (LLMs). Its legal system combines inherited English common law with jurisdiction-specific statutes, requiring models to distinguish local doctrine from generic common-law intuition. This setting also highlights the challenge of recognizing underspecification in lay legal queries, because the facts material to a legal outcome depend on the governing doctrine. Yet legal benchmarks rarely cover Singapore law or test this form of ambiguity recognition. To address these gaps, we introduce SG-LegalClarify, a large-scale benchmark for open-ended legal reasoning and ambiguity recognition in Singapore law. SG-LegalClarify contains 1,100 lawyer-authored source questions spanning 10 legal domains, including 340 fully specified and 760 underspecified questions. Each underspecified question has a fixed hidden-fact assignment and a fully specified counterpart, yielding 1,860 evaluation instances. Responses are graded with lawyer-authored Issue, Rule, Application, and Conclusion (IRAC) rubrics. We evaluate 19 LLMs, closed-book and with web search, using a multi-turn pipeline in which models decide whether to answer or clarify, and a user simulator reveals hidden facts only when asked. We find the benchmark far from saturated: the best models satisfy only 69.8% of mandatory rubric items closed-book (average 53.8%) and 77.8% with web search (average 63.0%). Models also struggle to recognize when clarification is necessary. We will release the public split of our benchmark, the model outputs on it, and the evaluation pipeline to support future research.

title_en: When AI Agents Should Repair, Replan, or Abandon: A Threshold Theory of Plan Commitment
abstract_en: AI agents often discover mid-execution that their plan is broken, for example when an action fails or a tool is withdrawn. Deployed systems use conventions such as retry loops or "always replan," and a recent benchmark finds no fixed strategy dominates. This paper derives the optimal policy. In the model, a disruption destroys the causal support of part of a plan; repair is a partial reset that preserves the plan's structure, replanning is a full reset, and changing a plan is costly because others have conditioned on it. The optimal policy is a threshold in effective disruption depth: repair shallow damage, replan after deep damage, and abandon the goal when even a fresh plan is not worth its cost. Depth depends on plan structure. In expectation, a single broken action forces 1+R(G)/n actions to be revalidated, where R(G) counts the pairs of actions joined by a dependency path; to first order, a fully serial plan switches to replanning at raw damage about w times smaller than a plan of w parallel chains. A closed-form stability-price threshold determines when a worse repaired plan should be kept over a better fresh one. As language-model planners push replanning costs toward zero, the stability price becomes the only force sustaining plan commitment. Under repeated disruptions, revision frictions make commitment hysteresis optimal: the agent keeps executing a plan it would never choose fresh, and each repair adds patch debt until the debt outweighs repair's cost advantage and the agent rebuilds. A value-of-diagnosis result states when measuring damage is worth its compute and shows that "always replan" is optimal when damage is predictably deep and replanning is the better fallback. A separately implemented numerical checker tests each proposition (zero violations; 1.6 million static-model evaluations), and the model's regime map reproduces that benchmark's regime flips qualitatively.

title_en: With the Right Representation, Classical Machine Learning Rivals Deep Models for Olfactory Mixture Similarity
abstract_en: Modeling olfactory mixtures remains a critical challenge in machine olfaction because the task requires reasoning over relationships between sets of odorants rather than over individual molecules in isolation. However, prior comparisons between deep and classical approaches also varied how the relationship between the two mixtures was represented, since the classical baselines primarily relied on weak representations that described each mixture independently and provided little direct signal about how the mixtures differed. In this work, we revisit classical learning using explicit symmetric comparison features on unordered pairs of mixtures, evaluating these representations with XGBoost and kernel ridge regression (KRR). We find that XGBoost with explicit comparison features achieves performance competitive with specialized deep mixture models on the main benchmark. Ablation studies show that coordinate-wise absolute differences alone provide strong predictive performance, while combining them with sums and products yields further improvements. KRR also benefits substantially from explicit comparison features, with further gains from appropriate kernel choice and preprocessing. Overall, these results suggest that explicitly encoding how two mixtures differ is an important ingredient for classical machine learning in low-data olfactory mixture prediction.

title_en: ROUNDS: Source-Framed Diagnostic Revision after Multi-Turn Clinical Evidence
abstract_en: Large language models (LLMs) achieve high scores on medical benchmarks, but does this performance translate into reliable diagnosis as a conversation unfolds? In diagnostic conversations, users can provide clinical findings across multiple turns, ask for a diagnosis without supplying answer options, and introduce opinions from others. Models must therefore form diagnoses from the available evidence and decide how to respond to subsequent advice. We introduce ROUNDS, a framework that evaluates these abilities after a fixed sequence of clinical evidence delivered over multiple turns. ROUNDS compares diagnosis with and without answer options, presents the same incorrect diagnosis under clinician and lay framing, and varies support for competing diagnoses in written five-clinician panels. Clinician-framed misleading advice produced lower final accuracy than lay-framed advice in every model, with differences of 4.6 to 38.2 percentage points. Initially correct diagnoses more often became incorrect answers than abstentions, and many adopted the suggested disease. Conversely, accuracy increased as more panel members supported the correct diagnosis, including when the majority opinion remained unchanged. title_en: Well-Log Reconstruction with Pre-trained Geological Knowledge: A Knowledge-Conditioned Large-Language-Model Generative Agent
abstract_en: Missing well-log intervals make subsurface reconstruction ill-posed. Existing numerical regression models lack geological prior knowledge to constrain ambiguous inverse mappings. We propose GeoLog-Agent, a knowledge-conditioned generative agent using pre-trained large language models (LLMs) as a source of geological priors. A universal Geo-Harness translates LLM stratigraphic reasoning into formation-anchored petrophysical trajectories, feature-wise linear modulation, and conditional adversarial constraints. On the Norwegian North Sea benchmark, GeoLog-Agent achieves a mean $R^2$ of 0.9307 and a peak $R^2$ of 0.9713. It exceeds the nine-baseline average $R^2$ of 0.8387 by 0.0920, with a 30.97% average RMSE reduction, and exceeds the strongest baseline by 0.0274--0.0498 in $R^2$, with 16.25%--24.05% lower RMSE. Ablations confirm the effectiveness and synergy of geological prior reasoning, multi-scale dilated generation, and conditional adversarial modules. Transferring the coupling mechanism to six conventional deep learning models improves their $R^2$ by 0.0162--0.0789 with cross-well stability. These results demonstrate how foundation-model domain reasoning can constrain deep generative reconstruction of missing petrophysical measurements.

title_en: Data-Driven Heuristic-Guided Business Process Redesign
abstract_en: Business process redesign (BPR) has a long-standing catalog of best-practice redesign heuristics, yet, applying them remains a mostly manual task that requires extensive domain knowledge. Despite recent advances using Large Language Models (LLMs) for conversational process model redesign, limitations remain. For example, redesign is user-driven instead of data-driven and is not guided by best practices such as the redesign heuristics. Moreover, only one change can be handled at a time. To address these limitations, given an event log and a BPMN model, we present the DH-BPR framework to realize data-driven heuristic-guided BPR using LLMs. To design DH-BPR, we first conducted an analysis of which redesign heuristics can be automatically detected and applied given information contained in an event log such as the fraction of cases that bypass an activity. Based on this, DH-BPR detects and validates heuristic candidates through a combination of rule-based techniques and an LLM. After that, DH-BPR jointly designs and records an application plan for valid candidates, before finally yielding a redesigned BPMN model and an updated resource model (the way resources execute the process). Evaluation based on simulation using a synthetic benchmark and two real-world event logs shows that the framework's redesign reduces the mean case completion time by up to 61.5%.

title_en: A Hierarchical Statistical Framework for Evaluating Agent Reliability
abstract_en: Agents operating in complex scenarios often face uncertainty due to incomplete information about the environment they operate in, ambiguous user queries, complex business rules and the inherently stochastic dynamics of the governing policy. Several new benchmarks have been proposed to evaluate LLM-based agents on complex tasks in multi-tool environments, including settings with policy constraints and varying levels of intent ambiguity. These conditions make it important to evaluate agentic systems systematically and quantify their performance under different conditions to assess their reliability in production. This need is evident in the recently introduced Thinkingbox benchmark, where even the strongest models struggle to perform consistently across diverse business scenarios. This paper presents a statistical framework for evaluating uncertainty and reliability in agentic systems. We define a hierarchy of scenarios, instances, and samples to assess model performance and variability systematically. We apply this framework to common metrics found in the literature: mean pass rate, $pass@k$, and $passhat^k$, with uncertainty estimates for each metric. Aggregating metrics at different levels of the hierarchy reveals different structures and properties of the policy model; we connect this hierarchical aggregation with the known process of \emph{coarse-graining} as intended in the physics and statistical literature. We independently derive exact finite-sample expressions for the sampling variances of the unbiased $pass@k$ and $passhatk$ estimators; related results also appear in recent submissions. Our central contribution is a constructive derivation of hierarchical uncertainty propagation, making explicit its correspondence with coarse-graining and separating execution noise from task heterogeneity.

title_en: RTLReviewBench: LLM Hardware Reviewers Rarely Miss Bugs but Routinely Reject Correct RTL
abstract_en: Hardware teams increasingly ask large language models (LLMs) to review register-transfer level (RTL) code, yet it is unclear whether a model can tell a correct module from a buggy one without simulating it. We introduce RTLReviewBench, a benchmark of 114 matched pairs of buggy and correct Verilog modules. Each pair shares one specification, most buggy modules are real failures of LLM code generators, and every label is confirmed by simulation. Evaluating 12 commercial and open-weight models, we find a consistent asymmetry: reviewers rarely accept buggy code but often reject correct code, producing more than five false rejections for every missed bug. Synthetic mutants hide part of the problem: on the same designs, models miss far fewer injected bugs than real ones. Asking a model to reason before it commits to a verdict sharply reduces false rejections for weaker reviewers, and a controlled ablation shows that where the reasoning appears in the output matters more than the instruction to reason, whereas sampling and majority voting do not help. A blinded audit further shows that some correct "buggy" verdicts rest on false technical claims. We release the benchmark, a harder split for future models, all model responses, and the evaluation code at https://github.com/yasirmahmud/RTLReviewBench

title_en: Toward Planning Representations That Separate Task Structure from Visual Content
abstract_en: Effective planning requires representations that preserve task-relevant geometry and object identity while ignoring visual variation that does not alter the task. Existing evaluations of visual generalization often change several factors simultaneously, making the source of a failure difficult to identify. We introduce a controlled evaluation of object-goal navigation (ObjectNav), the task of reaching an instance of a named object category, in procedurally generated ProcTHOR houses. Training and evaluation houses share floor plans, object locations, goals, and start states, while visual factors are changed individually or in combination. Across model-free reinforcement learning (RL), model-based RL, and agents using frozen pretrained visual representations, our results show that appearance changes impair navigation, but their effects differ sharply by factor. Surface material changes account for most of the average change in success, whereas clutter and lighting have little effect. The magnitude of a global image statistics shift does not reliably predict performance: changing only the goal object's appearance can substantially impair an end-to-end agent despite a small image-level change. We found that a model based agent that plans over frozen features from the pretrained DINOv2 image encoder achieves the highest success (0.83) under the full shift, but remains sensitive to surface appearance. Our experiments reveal an important requirement for planning representations: they must separate invariant spatial task structure from appearance.

title_en: SemMask: Semantic-Prioritized Progressive Masking for Diffusion Language Models
abstract_en: Diffusion Language Models (DLMs) are designed to enable globally parallel generation. However, in practice, they often exhibit pseudo-autoregressive behavior and a function-word-first bias, which undermines their performance on tasks such as text writing and code generation that benefit from global planning and parallel decoding. To address this, we propose SemMask, a novel fine-tuning paradigm that leverages a semantic-prioritized progressive masking strategy to encourage the model to decode high-information semantic tokens early and globally, thereby enhancing its global planning and parallel generation capabilities. Specifically, we first use the gradients of the original DLM with respect to each token to identify semantic tokens. During masking, these semantic tokens are preserved with priority, establishing a progressive generation order in which semantic tokens are decoded prior to function tokens. Meanwhile, we adjust the loss weight for semantic tokens to further reinforce their early prediction. Experimental results show that SemMask achieves quality comparable to strong autoregressive baselines on both text writing and code generation tasks, while providing superior semantic coherence. Notably, SemMask achieves higher accuracy with substantially fewer decoding steps, indicating that the early establishment of semantic structure improves the efficiency--accuracy trade-off.

title_en: Synthetic Neurosymbolic Task Generation with Controlled Constraint Complexity
abstract_en: We introduce NeSySy, a synthetic generator for neurosymbolic learning tasks that jointly produces logical constraints and consistent datasets. Unlike existing benchmarks, NeSySy provides fine-grained control over key properties such as constraint structure, tightness, input dependence, and data generation and alignment strategies. In particular, it allows the use of rich constraints over infinite domains, and uses solvers to ensure that the constraints are meaningful and that generated samples satisfy the constraints. We design NeSySy to support both learning with declarative constraints and learning from distant supervision. Across a range of constraint families, we provide evidence that its parameters induce systematic and largely independent effects on task difficulty. Using NeSySy, we study constraint-aware learning methods, identifying regimes where explicit constraint enforcement is beneficial and where expressive unconstrained models can instead learn constraint structure directly from data. Our results establish NeSySy as a controlled testbed for analysing the interaction between learning and logical structure. NeSySy is built around a pipeline that incorporates solvers. Satisfiability checkers (CNFgen and Z3) generate and certify constraints. Constrained optimizers (RC2 for MaxSAT, Z3 for OMT) compute optimal repairs that guarantee every generated sample is consistent.

title_en: PBit1: One Programmable P-Bit per Parameter - A Finite-Control Representation of Pretrained Networks
abstract_en: We introduce PBit1, a finite-control representation of pretrained neural networks that assigns one programmable p-bit to each learned parameter. A 12-bit command sets its probability, a shared affine range maps that probability to the weight domain, and temporal observations reconstruct the weight for inference. Operator-aware range grouping and sensitivity-based sampling allocation adapt the representation to the network. Across five independent weight draws at 32,768 observations per scalar, selected configurations preserve task quality in GPT-2, DistilBERT, and LFM3-1.7B with every learned scalar converted and no fine-tuning. GPT-2 and LFM3 perplexity increase by approximately 0.66% and 0.26%, respectively, while DistilBERT accuracy changes from 87.51% to 87.49%. A sensitivity-based policy reduces GPT-2 reconstruction observations by 41.7% while retaining the quality criterion. Complete-model evaluations reuse reconstructed weights in BF16 inference, and THRML operator experiments examine native sampling and spatial-temporal tradeoffs. Together, these results establish PBit1 as a concrete construction for studying finite-control weight representation and temporal reconstruction in pretrained networks.

title_en: Behavioral Assurance for Socially Deployed AI Agents
abstract_en: AI agents are increasingly deployed in socially consequential settings, yet existing evaluations provide limited assurance that they behave consistently with their intended characteristics across diverse interactions. We introduce an evaluation framework for measuring the behavioral consistency of socially deployed AI agents. The framework operationalizes agent behavior along five measurable axes and uses a standardized evaluation battery spanning six socially salient interaction settings to assess behavioral differentiation, consistency, and drift. Controlled persona configurations serve as experimental anchors, enabling systematic testing of whether intended behavioral differences persist across contexts rather than appearing only as stylistic variation. Preliminary analyses demonstrate measurable differentiation across configurations and suggest associations between behavioral profiles and interaction outcomes. By shifting the focus from persona design to behavioral assurance, this work provides a foundation for evaluating whether socially deployed AI agents behave as intended, consistently and measurably, across the situations in which users encounter them.

title_en: Inquest: Log-Guided Root-Cause Code Localization with a Staged Agent
abstract_en: When a production issue is reported, engineers get a description and some logs, but no failing test and no way to reproduce the fault. The logs show where the failure was noticed, not where it was caused: in 49% of the real reports we study, the text names none of the files that the fix later changed. We built a benchmark for this setting from two public datasets and 27 open-source projects (Apache, Red Hat, MongoDB, MariaDB, Qt and Sakai). It holds 38,001 resolved issue reports with their pasted logs, the code as it was while the bug was still present, and the files the fix changed. We present INQUEST, an agent that finds the faulty code using a 27B open-weights model. Code, not the model, controls the procedure. It first gathers the evidence, including the files fixed in similar past issues that were resolved before the report was filed. The model then makes only three bounded decisions: which files to open, what role each file plays in the failure, and how to rank them. On 26,544 evaluation reports, INQUEST ranks a changed file first for 68.6% and in the top five for 85.9%, names the correct module for 90.2%, and ranks a changed function first for 53.8%. On the reports that name no faulty file, it reaches 52.8% and 73.6%. A free agent loop with the same model and tools finds files equally well, but names the faulty function 14 points less often. On a 1,000-report sample, INQUEST beats our reimplementations of two published agents by 7 and 20 points of top-1 accuracy (4 and 16 counting only the reports those agents answered), and the same model used as a re-ranker by 6. We report the cost of every system and the results that go against us, and we release the benchmark, both systems and every run transcript.

title_en: EndoComparer: Comparative Surgical Video Question Answering with Pseudo-Siamese Visual Adaptation and Perceive-then-Compare Reasoning
abstract_en: Purpose: Surgical training benefits from explicit comparison between cases: in patient condition, in technique and in skill proficiency. Surgical vision-language models (VLMs) offer a promising and flexible interface for this purpose. Yet current VLMs typically see one video at a time, and they often fall short when asked to compare videos. Methods: We propose EndoComparer, a VLM for comparative surgical video question answering with two components. (a) A Pseudo-Siamese Visual LoRA (PSVL) gives each video slot its own low-rank adapter over a shared frozen vision encoder, separating the two videos in the visual pathway at the cost of a single encoder pass. (b) A Perceive-then-Compare chain of thought (PtC-CoT) trains the model to first state what each video shows, then derive the answer from these statements. We further curate EndoDiffVQA, a benchmark of nearly 11K multiple-choice questions on video-pair over cholecystectomy and gastric bypass procedures, covering anatomy, tool, action and skill. Results: EndoComparer outperforms strong generalist and surgical VLMs on detecting and specifying difference between videos. Ablations show that two proposed components contribute complimentarily, and the model remains more robust under a video-swap control that exposes confusion between the two videos. Conclusion: Providing a dedicated visual reasoning path through PSVL and PtC-CoT makes cross-case comparison of surgical videos more robust for VLMs. EndoDiffVQA and EndoComparer provide a benchmark and a strong baseline for this task. title_en: Objectify, Don't Delete: Complaint-Derived Evaluation of Ambient Clinical Notes
abstract_en: Evaluating the quality of AI-generated clinical notes is hard: standard metrics like ROUGE measure lexical similarity to reference notes, while expert checklists encode what committees believe matters. Neither captures what clinicians actually complain about. Recent work has shown that evaluation criteria can be mined from user feedback and filtered to criteria that LLM judges can reliably enforce. We argue that this is where much of the value is lost. The criteria that fail enforceability are disproportionately the ones clinicians raise most often, because high-frequency complaints are stated as several questions glued together. No yes/no judgment can grade such composites as posed. We introduce an objectification step that rewrites such criteria into sets of scoped, determinate decisions. We demonstrate the approach through an evaluation pipeline that mines criteria from complaints, objectifies them, and deploys LLM judges against both planted defects and production notes. Across eleven defects planted into ACI-bench reference notes, objectified judges localize violations with median recall of 0.95, while reference metrics change by at most 0.037. Given the complaint as one broad question, the same judges still find every planted defect, but they also flag 70% of the unperturbed reference notes; one section-pair question per call raises Youden's J from 0.30 to 0.72 (by 0.19 to 0.26 with prompt effort matched). We release ACI-Defect, a perturbation benchmark; clinician-reviewed instance-level labels showing quality gaps in the ACI-bench gold standard (32 of 40 notes contain hallucinations; 40 of 40 omit discussed facts); and grounding-judge verdicts. On 1,446 production notes, mean instance-rate burden falls at every clinician-rating step (rho=-0.15), a small association. Defect counts have to be kept per span rather than collapsed into one pass/fail bit per note.

title_en: Evaluating and Improving Natural Language Autoencoders
abstract_en: Natural language autoencoders (NLAs) are a method for generating natural language explanations of LLM activations. We develop evaluations based on auditing tasks that test the ability of NLAs to surface latent knowledge, identify whether a model was misled by a hint, and catch a silent fabrication. We also develop extensions to NLAs that let them use activation information from multiple layers and positions, let us apply them more effectively to long transcripts, and reduce the number of false claims they make. These extensions result in improvements on both our auditing evaluations and auxiliary evaluations adapted from prior work. We also use the evaluations to study how different auditing capabilities change over the course of NLA training, and find that although every evaluation improves early in training, extended training can hurt performance on some of our auditing evaluations.

title_en: Beyond Prompts: Runtime Contracts for Coding Agents
abstract_en: Coding agents act on repositories through shell commands and file edits, and teams steer them with written engineering rules. Industrial settings expect such rules to be enforced and their application to be evidenced, and a rule given as prompt text provides neither. We test whether executable contracts enforced while the agent works reduce rule violations compared with the same rules in the prompt, retrieved as guidance, or checked only after generation. Violations are scored by an oracle whose methods differ from the in-loop checks, and the oracle is validated by two human reviewers and a model reviewer. Across three studies on two model families (240, 112 and 108 runs), enforcement during execution produced no oracle-detected violation in 104 paired runs, against 21 to 55% of runs without rules, and no loss of functional correctness in the two confirmatory studies. In the confirmatory study on tasks aimed at known failure situations (Study 3, protocol hashed before the first run), enforcement lowered the share of violating runs by 31 percentage points relative to no rules (Holm-adjusted p = 0.014); the 17-point difference from prompted rules was not significant (p = 0.12), and neither was any contrast in Study 2, where only 3 of 14 tasks produced a violation. Prompted rules removed some violation types but not recursive deletes of scratch directories, and checks after generation repaired file edits but not commands that had already run. That enforcement satisfies the rules it enforces is expected by construction; what the data add is where prompting falls short, the absence of a functional cost, and the limits of the rules and of the oracle themselves. The studies use low-cost models and one small fixture.

title_en: Func-JEPA: Learning a Sobolev Space of Functions as Latent Vectors
abstract_en: Pretraining an encoder once and reusing it across tasks is a widespread approach in vision and language. However, neural symbolic mathematics still trains a dedicated sequence-to-sequence model for each task, so that no representation of a function is shared. In this work, we propose the Function Joint-Embedding Predictive Architecture (Func-JEPA, abbreviated f-JEPA): an encoder of mathematical functions, pretrained on their symbolic form, whose latent space imitates the Sobolev space H^1 and in which differentiation is a learned latent operator. The norm of a latent is computed exactly from the function, whereas its direction is learned to match Sobolev angles. The frozen encoder is then reused by lightweight modules for decoding, composition, integration, and regression from samples. The representation and four downstream tasks are evaluated within and outside the pretraining distribution. f-JEPA recovers exact formulas from noisy samples more often than the compared symbolic-regression methods, whereas computer algebra and task-specific models remain stronger on standard integration and differential-equation benchmarks.

title_en: Agent Authenticator: Passkey-Grade, Hardware-Bound Authentication for AI Agents
abstract_en: AI coding agents now push code, publish packages, call model APIs and operate cloud resources on behalf of developers. They authenticate to these services with the same bearer secrets humans use, personal access tokens, API keys and package-registry tokens, stored where the model, its subprocesses and any co-resident malware can read them. Incidents in 2025 and 2026, including prompt-injection attacks on coding agents and self-propagating supply-chain worms, show that this arrangement fails in predictable ways. Passkeys solved the analogous problem for humans, but they require a human gesture on every use and cannot be operated by an autonomous process. We present the Agent Authenticator, a design that gives agents passkey-grade authentication properties: per-service hardware-bound keys, no shared secrets, origin binding enforced by the runtime rather than the model, normalized attestation of the execution environment, human-signed scoped mandates, and cross-device human approval for high-risk actions. The same protocol serves agents on developer laptops and in cloud enclaves, and it deploys as a profile over existing mechanisms, MCP authorization, OAuth token exchange including the Identity Assertion JWT Authorization Grant, git and SSH, rather than as a new identity system. The authenticator also produces a signed, hash-chained record of each action it authorizes. We analyze the design against a threat model centered on prompt injection and same-host compromise, map it onto five documented incidents, and discuss its limits.

title_en: LLM Trading Agents Earn Beta, Not Alpha: A Look-Ahead-Free Benchmark
abstract_en: Large language model (LLM) trading agents now trade stocks for their users, and benchmarks rank models by their agents' returns. Yet a single run's return says little about skill. In our study, two runs of the same model that differed only in the random seed ended 5.2 points apart on average, so telling skill from luck takes many backtests across markets, models and seeds. However, live arenas trade each day only once, and backtests either use the few months after a model's training cutoff or run on years the model may remember, often with news joined to prices by calendar date. In this paper, we present rta-bench-1, a backtest over three US markets (a rally, a bear market and a crash). It shows each headline only after its publication minute, plays each period blind and named, and checks every run for look-ahead. It also splits each return into factor exposure and alpha and scores every decision against random choices of the same day and sector. In 91 runs of six models from four vendors, no alpha was significant, market and style exposure accounted for a median 78% of the return, and the decisions did no better than random stocks of the same sector. The agents bought the stocks with the most positive news, yet in ablations they earned as much without their headlines. Still, the agents carried out rules reliably, since a single cash rule in the prompt cut a GPT-based agent's share in stocks by 30.3 points in all six pairs. Builders should therefore supply the edge themselves and report exposures and alpha, and benchmarks should replay news by publication time.

title_en: Equilibrium measures for anisotropic exponential interaction energies with applications to transformers
abstract_en: We study the minimization of anisotropic exponential interaction energies over probability measures on the sphere, motivated by mean-field models of self-attention in transformer architectures. For every symmetric positive definite interaction matrix, we relate the minimizer to a corresponding anisotropic Brownian motion and use the Feynman--Kac formula and elliptic regularity theory to show that it admits a smooth, strictly positive density on the sphere. We further show that it is the only stationary measure with full support for the dynamics considered. We use the stochastic viewpoint to derive an algorithm for sampling from the minimizer. In dimension two, we also propose a numerical scheme for approximating its density based on a Mathieu series expansion.

title_en: Over-the-Air Semantic Alignment via Dual Stacked Intelligent Metasurfaces
abstract_en: Semantic communications enable task-oriented information exchange, but suffer from latent-space mismatch when transmitter and receiver employ heterogeneous machine learning models. Existing semantic alignment methods rely on digital processing, introducing computational and latency overhead. This paper proposes a dual stacked intelligent metasurfaces (dual-SIM) architecture that performs semantic alignment entirely in the wave domain. By jointly exploiting programmable metasurfaces at both ends of a link and the wireless channel, the proposed architecture realizes an end-to-end linear transformation between heterogeneous latent spaces. We show phase-only multilayer SIM can approximate both supervised linear aligners and zero-shot Parseval-frame equalizers. We investigate single-SIM, disjoint asymmetric and symmetric dual-SIM, and jointly optimized dual-SIM configurations, considering channel equalization and constructive channel exploitation. For joint design, we develop an alternating projected gradient algorithm with convergence guarantees to first-order stationary points. We further introduce a deep-unrolled network that unrolls gradient-based iterations to reduce computational cost of SIM reconfiguration under channel variations. Numerical results with heterogeneous vision transformer encoders show accurate semantic alignment from moderate to high signal-to-noise ratios. The joint and symmetric disjoint dual-SIM designs achieve the highest accuracy over compact channels, the joint design leads at shallow stack depths, and the advantage over single-SIM designs diminishes at equal depth.

title_en: PathLoop: Self-Evolving Multi-Agent Reasoning for Evidence-Grounded Whole-Slide Image Analysis
abstract_en: Analyzing whole-slide images (WSIs) requires combining evidence across tissue regions and spatial scales. Multi-agent systems offer a promising approach to this task. However, existing systems make limited use of molecular evidence, often select visually prominent but less representative regions while overlooking global context, and struggle to reuse experience from previous cases. To address these challenges, we present PathLoop, a self-evolving multi-agent framework that integrates omics data for evidence-grounded WSI analysis. Specifically, PathLoop coordinates visual and omics interpreters across slide, patch, and pixel levels, using molecular signals to guide region selection and combining local tissue details with global slide features. A judgment agent then checks the consistency of the collected evidence against Pathology-Wiki, a knowledge base built from 48 entries across 24 organ systems, and triggers re-examination when the evidence is inconsistent. To reuse past experience, a four-level memory stores reasoning trajectories, practical tips, skills, and tools to guide future cases, forming a loop of evidence collection, review, and memory update. We evaluate PathLoop on four TCGA cohorts with biomarker prediction, survival prediction, and subtype classification. The results demonstrate the effectiveness of PathLoop across these tasks and support its use for evidence-grounded WSI analysis.

title_en: DBHiCo: Dual-Branch Hierarchical Contrastive Learning for MRI Image Classification
abstract_en: Automated Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) image classification provides a crucial non-invasive approach for neurological diagnosis, yet it is fundamentally challenged by inherent acquisition noise and high inter-subject structural similarity, which obscure subtle pathological variations, thereby limiting the performance of deep neural networks. While contrastive learning (CL) offers a promising mitigation strategy, existing paradigms rely on rigid binary partitions that ignore negative sample heterogeneity, and they fail to capture the cross-view structural consistency vital for fine-grained anatomical alignment. To address these barriers, we propose Dual-Branch Hierarchical Contrastive Learning (DBHiCo), a novel framework explicitly designed to collaboratively enforce structural consistency and semantic discrimination. Specifically, DBHiCo leverages a natural anatomical multi-view pair (original and skull-stripped MRI scans), processing them through a dual-branch architecture to seamlessly integrate holistic structural robustness with localized intracranial details. Crucially, we introduce a hierarchical contrastive loss that discards conventional binary constraints in favor of a margin-ranked similarity hierarchy. This mechanism explicitly orders positive and negative pairs based on their structural and semantic difficulty, thereby amplifying the fine-grained semantic discriminability of the learned representations. Extensive experiments across three diverse neurological datasets demonstrate that DBHiCo achieves state-of-the-art performance, consistently outperforming existing MRI multi-view representation learning and advanced contrastive fine-tuning methods.

title_en: Do Probing and Steering Favor the Same Directions Within and Across Language Models?
abstract_en: A direction in a language model's hidden state can be used to probe whether a concept is present or to steer the model toward it. Although probe directions are often reused for steering, the direction that best detects a concept need not be the one that best changes it. We study this distinction in three instruction-tuned models from different families. We construct a one-parameter family of directions ranging from a covariance-adjusted discriminant to the mean difference, and evaluate probing and additive steering, which adds the direction to the hidden state, along the family at a fixed side effect. For truthfulness and sentiment, in every model, the best probe is not the best steering direction: steering consistently favors directions closer to the mean difference. This separation holds across 59 of 60 layer-model-concept combinations in a layer sweep, with matched probe and steering texts in all six model-concept combinations, and under a rotation-based steering operator. The exact steering optimum is less stable: for sentiment, an intermediate direction produces a 27-56% stronger steering effect than the mean difference, but this gain shrinks or disappears with matched texts and depends on the layer and the operator. The two roles also transfer differently across models. A probe transferred by a linear map fitted on neutral text retains 81-91% of the target model's above-chance probing performance, while the transferred mean difference retains less of its steering effect in 11 of 12 model pairs. This is a consistent tendency, although our predefined criteria classify only three pairs, and nine remain inconclusive. Finally, as an application on PopQA, steering toward "unknown" increases abstention by 18-44 percentage points on uncertain errors, versus 2-5 on confident errors, while rarely correcting errors in cases where a correct answer is reachable.

title_en: Text Speeding Itself Up: Recency and Restraint in Session-Local Drafting
abstract_en: Speculative decoding lets a cheap draft model propose tokens that a large language model verifies in a single forward pass. When the verifier keeps a KV cache, verification is cheap and drafting must be nearly free. Session-local drafters, which predict from the prompt and the text generated so far, meet that bar without training. We compare a recency-weighted, backing-off, confidence-gated session memory against prompt lookup decoding in its reference form, which copies from the earliest earlier match, and in a variant that copies from the most recent one, with paired per-prompt bootstrap intervals throughout. On general, medical, and legal text with a Mistral-7B verifier, recency accounts for the speed: most-recent lookup gains up to 0.09 in speedup over earliest-match lookup on 500-token generations, and session memory's weighting and backoff add nothing measurable on top, at 30 to 40 times the drafting cost. Energy tells a different story. On medical and legal text, unselective drafters are 14% faster than plain decoding yet use as much energy per token, while drafters that abstain on weak evidence save 3 to 4 joules per 100 tokens; a three-token minimum match length on prompt lookup matches the confidence-gated session memory. Outputs are token-identical to greedy decoding in 94% of generations, with every divergence at a numerical near-tie. Under a repetition penalty, long-generation speedups shrink from 1.4-1.7x to 1.1-1.2x, but recency still helps and the length floor is the only drafter that saves energy in both domains.

title_en: InvarOrd: Self-Supervised Ordinal Knowledge Distillation with Rank-Invariant Alignment for Label-Efficient Cross-Species Hyperspectral Fish Freshness Assessment
abstract_en: Hyperspectral models of fish freshness rarely transfer between species, and labelling a new species is slow and destructive. Freshness is also ordinal, and standard domain alignment can erase that order. We present InvarOrd, which adapts to a new species from 30 labelled cubes (5 per rank) in three stages: self-supervised spectral pretraining on unlabelled source cubes, cross-species alignment by a shrinkage covariance discrepancy computed only within matched ranks, and ordinal distillation into a compact student. The alignment term is provably invariant to the rank means, so it gives no incentive to collapse the ordinal axis. On paired salmon and cod data (800 cubes each, 16 days), a source-trained teacher reaches 1.6 to 1.9 days mean absolute error (MAE) on the other species, with quadratic weighted kappa (QWK) below zero. The 423K-parameter student, 2.54 times smaller than its teacher, attains the lowest MAE (1.476 days) and highest within 1-day accuracy (56.1%) among 14 configurations, matching the best of six ImageNet-pretrained backbones (ConvNeXt-T, 1.503 days) at 66 times fewer parameters, 1.44ms per cube on a GPU and 5s re-adaptation. InvarOrd beats target-only training by 0.29 days (p = 0.031). Among alignment objectives, rank-invariant alignment retains the most ordinal structure (embedding rank correlation 0.183, QWK 0.112), whereas global discrepancy lowers the rank correlation to 0.049 and QWK to zero at only 0.014 days higher MAE.

title_en: Program Distillation: Transferring LLM Capability from System 2 to System 0
abstract_en: Recent studies leverage large language models (LLMs) to construct executable programs through environment interaction, feedback analysis, and code revision. However, prior work has mainly treated LLMs as optimizers, overlooking their ability to transfer knowledge across system levels. We propose Program Distillation (PD), a framework that formalizes the transfer of abilities from System 2 to System 0. During learning, the LLM provides task knowledge and draft strategies; at deployment, a student program executes the resulting policy. We show that this approach can improve performance while reducing inference time. We introduce PDBench, a benchmark comprising 27 discrete- and continuous-control tasks with fixed initial policies, and PDMetaHarness, a model-harness-independent meta-system for monitoring and guiding the learning process. The strongest model achieves a normalized mean score of 0.728, surpassing PPO (0.656) and Jev-like decision models (0.239), while running exclusively on CPUs and reducing inference costs. Our analysis shows that performance is largely driven by the first breakthrough during learning, and structural modifications have a slightly lower success rate than parameter modifications but typically yield larger gains. We further introduce style distillation, which enables interpretable stylistic control over the learning process. Overall, we present an analytical framework for PD and demonstrate its practical viability.

title_en: CLEW: Log-Anchored Backward Tracing for Root-Cause Code Localization
abstract_en: Failures in industrial software systems may involve multiple components and be difficult to reproduce outside the production environment. Root-cause code localization therefore often relies on issue descriptions and runtime logs. However, log evidence may be noisy or incomplete, and the code reporting a symptom may differ from the code containing the underlying defect. These conditions make it challenging to identify relevant log evidence and determine which functions could have caused the reported failure. To address this gap, we introduce CLEW, an agentic approach that combines rule-based log-to-code anchoring with LLM-guided backward code tracing. CLEW organizes selected observations into diagnostic states, guides source exploration from anchored symptom functions, and returns ranked candidate functions, an affected module, and an explanation comprising a proposed mechanism path and associated log events. For evaluation, we construct LogLoc, a benchmark comprising 192 real-world issue and fault-injection cases. Against three baselines, CLEW records the highest observed Acc@1 (77.3%) and MRR (81.3%) on LogLoc-Issues and matches the leading baselines at 97.6% Acc@1 on LogLoc-Airflow. Averaged over all 192 cases, CLEW's wall-clock time is approximately 73% lower than LocAgent's at a similar average inference cost. No aggregate degradation is observed under the tested perturbations, with modest changes in Acc@1 and MRR across the evaluated seeds and base models. These results suggest that CLEW can combine function-level localization with evidence links and runtime efficiency under the evaluated conditions.

title_en: Interpreting Random Forests: Comparing Surrogate Models and Rule Extraction Methods
abstract_en: Random forests (RFs) often achieve high prediction performance, but their ensemble structure can be difficult to interpret. Surrogate models and rule extraction methods offer interpretable approximations, yet guidance on selecting an appropriate method for a specific research question remains limited. We compared 12 methods for interpreting RFs, with a decision tree as a prediction-oriented reference, across 11 simulation settings and 67 benchmark datasets for regression and classification. Evaluation addressed prediction and structural similarity to the RF, model complexity, prediction performance, and runtime. Simulations additionally assessed explainability using known effect and noise variables. No method performed best across all objectives. For regression, SLIM provided the strongest general performance for prediction similarity or performance on test data, while a linear model offered a simpler global interpretation of linear effects when performance was comparable. For classification, inTrees achieved the strongest overall benchmark performance, with CTree and OC-CART providing useful alternatives. ART consistently produced the most compact representations. NH and SIRUS offered strong structural similarity for regression, while MRT most closely reproduced RF variable usage in the classification simulations, illustrating that prediction-oriented rankings do not necessarily identify the best structural explanation. Outcome-type restrictions, runtime limits, and method-specific failures reduced result availability for several approaches and should be considered alongside performance when selecting a method. Method selection should therefore be guided by the outcome type, anticipated data structure, and intended interpretability objective. Prediction similarity alone is insufficient for explaining an RF and should be considered jointly with structural similarity and model complexity.

title_en: Successive Convexification in Learned World Models for Safe Offline Planning
abstract_en: World models learned from offline data allow an agent to plan without further interaction with the environment, but the sampling-based planners used with them handle safety constraints only by scoring or rejecting sampled action sequences. We instead pose safe planning in the latent space of a learned world model as a successive convex program (SCP), in which a learned discrete-time control barrier function is imposed as a constraint at every step of the horizon. SCP requires smooth dynamics, so we build the networks from smoothed MaxMin activations and spectrally normalised layers, and bound the resulting linearisation error in terms of the Lipschitz bound and the smoothing width. As SCP is a local method, we start it from a sampled plan. On two Safety-Gymnasium navigation tasks with offline data, this planner has fewer violations than MPPI and CEM drawing 128 times as many samples at equal wall-clock time in our main comparison, though not significantly, and earns greater return at longer horizons, and is much safer than SCP without a sampled start. SCP converged more often on Lipschitz-bounded models. Unlike sampling, it also reports at each step whether its plan is a feasible, first-order optimal KKT point of the planning problem in the model, or that no feasible plan was found nearby. Our implementation is publicly available at https://github.com/youngers2006/scwm.

title_en: Efficient and Accurate Causal Validation of Training Data Attribution
abstract_en: Causal validation of training data attribution (TDA) methods is costly, since evaluation involves retraining a model on many different subsets of the original training set. For example, the Linear Datamodeling Score (LDS), which has become a standard metric for evaluating TDA methods, measures the correlation between TDA predictions and expected retrained model outputs. In this paper, we reduce the amount of computation needed to estimate the LDS along three axes: the number of sampled training subsets, the number of retraining seeds per subset, and the number of models in the attribution ensemble. Each of these factors induces a form of bias in the LDS estimation, and removing these sources of bias significantly reduces the number of retrainings needed to match the same accuracy in LDS estimation. On ResNet-9/CIFAR-10, finite-subset debiasing achieves $3.2\%$ relative RMSE with as few as $4$ subsets, and $32$ subsets match the accuracy of ordinary Spearman using $96$ subsets, measured against a 300-subset reference. On ResNet-9/CIFAR-10, BERT/QNLI and GPT-2/WikiText-2, estimating the training-noise variance allows us to reproduce the standard five-seed LDS at the same accuracy with $2$--$5\times$ fewer retrainings.

title_en: Beyond Paired Inputs: Learning to Leverage RGB-T Cross-Modal Relations in Multimodal Large Language Models
abstract_en: RGB and thermal infrared (TIR) sensors provide complementary observations, yet their distinct sensing characteristics make effective cross-modal coordination challenging. Although existing multimodal large language models (MLLMs) can process paired RGB-T inputs, they often fail to translate cross-modal relations into effective task-specific decisions, leaving the potential of these relations to improve task performance and robustness largely untapped. Motivated by this observation, we introduce RelMLLM, an RGB-T MLLM that explicitly learns to exploit cross-modal relations in task-specific decision making. It represents modality reliability, the cross-modal relation, and the dominant modality as a verifiable decision state. We derive task-grounded supervision for this state by comparing RGB-only, TIR-only, and paired RGB-T task outcomes. A hierarchical relation-guided reward supervises modality-specific evidence, relation-state prediction, and the final task output, while encouraging consistency across evidence, relation, and decision. We evaluate RelMLLM on natural RGB-T grounding, RGB-T visual question answering, and held-out sensor degradation. RelMLLM improves grounding accuracy and degradation robustness over its Qwen3-VL baselines while preserving performance on general RGB-T reasoning benchmarks. These results demonstrate that effectively exploiting cross-modal relations leads to more accurate and robust RGB-T decisions. Code and model weights are publicly available.

title_en: StyleJudge: A Human-Validated, In-Context-Learning Vision-Language Evaluator for Artistic Style Transfer
abstract_en: Automatic evaluation of artistic style transfer remains an open problem: existing metrics score an image pair in isolation, without seeing an example of the intended style transformation, and correlate poorly with human judgment. We introduce StyleJudge, a compact vision-language evaluator conditioned on a small set of reference source-to-stylized pairs before scoring a query pair, mirroring how a human rater calibrates to a style before judging a candidate. On a human-annotated benchmark of 878 rated pairs across 12 artistic styles (728 from 10 training/validation styles, 150 from 2 unseen styles), our efficient 0.8B-parameter StyleJudge reaches a Pearson correlation of 0.291 (Spearman 0.325) with human ratings on seen styles and 0.381 on unseen ones. On seen styles, it achieves the highest positive correlation among tested metrics: Gram-matrix style loss and CLIP similarity correlate weakly ($r=0.041$, $r=0.168$), while LPIPS (scored higher when closer to the source) correlates negatively ($r=-0.404$). We achieve this by distilling evaluation knowledge from a 72B-parameter vision-language teacher used only during training, which reaches $r=0.327$, confirming that most of its human alignment survives compact distillation. For training, we build a dataset of source-to-stylized pairs across the 12 styles via LoRA-adapted diffusion, densified with graded intermediate examples from a high-resolution image-morphing pipeline so the evaluator recognizes partial and complete stylization. On two held-out validation styles, StyleJudge reaches 28.2% exact-match agreement with its teacher's structured scores versus 1.1% for the untuned base model, with 67.8% shorter reasoning traces, and scores a pair in 39 s (median) using 2.5 GB of GPU memory on one NVIDIA T4. We release the human-rating benchmark, annotation guideline, SDXL-adapted FreeMorph code, and model weights.

title_en: Semantics First, Pixels Later: Mission-Driven Event Streams for Drone Video over Bandwidth-Starved Links
abstract_en: A surveillance drone on a bandwidth-starved link cannot send the video its operator would need, yet the operator's questions are often not about pixels: did three people converge, when, and where? We study what should cross a link of 1 Mbps down to 1 kbps instead, and in what order. BPS, a behavior-primitive stream, sends semantics first and pixels later: it runs a detector and a tracker onboard and sends short records (25 bytes on average) of multi-frame events selected by a mission card of 16-125 bytes, ahead of positions and pictures. We measure it by what a ground-side language model answers from it, under a preregistered protocol with a held-out set, against H.265 read by the vision fine-tune of the same model, H.265 on which the ground runs our own perception, a stream of quantized tracks, and onboard captions. On the development set (84% of questions about convergence, mostly one location) the event stream answers 74.3% of questions at 0.13 kbps. A reader that receives nothing answers 57.4%, and the video reader 59.6% at 100 kbps and 64.7% on the source frames. When the ground instead runs our perception on the video, video matches the stream at 100 kbps, about 800 times the stream's rate, and falls behind at 64 kbps and below. A track stream matches it at 96 times the bytes and loses 0.03 at 17 times. On held-out data the result is weaker: with events taken from annotated tracks, an oracle, the stream beats H.265 at 100 kbps (+0.13), but with onboard perception it does not (+0.01 [-0.04, +0.06]) and is no better than receiving nothing. Sent alone through emulated links the event records answer 0.739 at 1 Mbps and still 0.724 at 0.3 kbps; an every-frame track stream holds down to 1 kbps and video with ground-side perception down to about 100 kbps. On a Jetson Orin Nano the unchanged pipeline runs at 4.5 fps and misses most events.

title_en: Do Rule-Based Tools Help LLMs Translate Endangered Uralic Languages in the Prompt or over MCP?
abstract_en: Komi-Zyrian, Moksha, Erzya and Udmurt have mature rule-based resources, among them finite-state analysers, constraint grammars and bilingual dictionaries, which language models do not use. We ask whether giving a model access to these resources improves machine translation from the four languages into English, and whether it matters how the access is provided: as analyses computed in advance and written into the prompt, or as tools that the model calls itself through the Model Context Protocol (MCP). We evaluate manually: an expert linguist read every English output of the strongest model under three conditions, 816 sentences in all, accepted or rejected each one, and named the main error in every rejected translation. With the analyses in the prompt, the number of accepted translations rises from 13 to 43 out of 272; with the tools attached it rises to 55. The gain comes from the bilingual dictionary. For Udmurt, whose dictionary has no English side, the prompt-based condition brings no gain at all, while for the other three languages an English gloss reaches the prompt for 74 to 80% of the source words. Tool calling is also much harder to get working than prompt injection. Of 31 open-weight models, 14 never call a tool, 11 of them because they cannot produce a usable call, and half of the calls that are made name a language the toolkit does not support. We release the data set, every model output and all tool-call logs.

title_en: Do Pretraining Optimizer Gains Transfer to KL Distillation?
abstract_en: Matrix-structured optimizers can improve language-model pretraining, but it is unclear whether these gains transfer to short-horizon KL distillation from an instruction-tuned initialization. We compare AdamW and diagonal AdaGrad with two tractable Shampoo reductions, SOAP, and All-2D Muon across four dense Qwen student-teacher pairs under a common forward-KL objective and fixed training budget. Across scales, none of the evaluated matrix-structured recipes consistently improves the quality versus trainer-time trade-off over the elementwise references: AdamW generally attains the lowest validation KL, while AdaGrad can be slightly faster at larger scale. SOAP often tracks AdamW in KL but incurs substantial trainer-time overhead, and the two Shampoo reductions reverse ordering across model pairs, showing that conclusions depend on the feasible recipe. These results suggest that pretraining optimizer gains do not transfer automatically to KL distillation and should be re-established for the target objective and systems regime.

title_en: PMR: MoE Routing with Shared Prototypes and Congestion Pricing
abstract_en: Conventional linear routers in sparse mixture-of-experts models select experts directly from token-expert matching scores, coupling input matching with expert allocation. We propose Prototype-Mediated Routing (PMR), a two-stage router with shared prototypes. PMR first computes each token's distribution over prototypes, then uses it to mix prototype-conditioned expert distributions according to the law of total probability. This formulation models input matching and expert allocation separately, explicitly represents many-to-many associations between prototypes and experts, and provides separate interfaces for context adaptation and load regulation. Within this framework, short-term states summarize preceding tokens to adapt the prototypes, while congestion prices updated from dispatch feedback achieve loss-free load balancing by adjusting the conditional expert distributions. We use a two-pass blockwise approximation to accelerate short-term state processing, achieving over 20 times the training throughput of the eager tokenwise PMR implementation while maintaining high agreement in routing decisions. Across three pretraining configurations with 0.43B, 1.18B, and 0.48B total parameters, PMR improves mean zero-shot accuracy on seven benchmarks over linear routing baselines with matched expert architectures by 1.54, 2.65, and 1.45 percentage points (pp), respectively. The corresponding gains on ARC-Easy are 6.71, 5.80, and 3.92 pp. In parameter-efficient fine-tuning of 7B-8B backbones, PMR's improvements over MixLoRA vary across backbones, with gains of up to 1.76 pp in mean accuracy across four tasks.

title_en: Confidence Without Cause: Predicting and Localizing Physics-Shortcut Sensitivity in Language Model Hidden States
abstract_en: A language model's confidence on a physics problem deserves trust only if it ignores details irrelevant to the answer. We introduce DECOY (Distractor-Embedded Certified cOunterfactuals for phYsics): 155 families of four prompts differing in one irrelevant detail. A symbolic solver certifies that each edit preserves the answer. Families are labelled by the largest drop in the model's log-probability of the certified answer, using a threshold fixed before probe training. Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct is sensitive on 50.0% of the 140 families yielding labels, and Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct on 22.9%. Effects are largest when distractor values lie numerically close to the answer. A linear probe on Qwen's layer-18 hidden state, averaged over four renderings, predicts sensitivity before generation at AUROC 0.760 with whole families held out. A separately tuned single-rendering probe reaches 0.747. A frozen layer-16 probe reaches 0.820 pooled AUROC on 15 families built after training, though within-cue-type AUROC is lower (0.667-0.6875). Under a paired family bootstrap, the probe performs on par with a fitted token-entropy baseline (AUROC 0.727) and achieves the lowest Brier score among tested predictors (0.204 versus 0.214). Knocking out four attention heads at layer 16 cancels sensitivity on a 20-family panel, localising it to a narrow mechanism. These results show that Qwen's confidence can track irrelevant details, that this failure is detectable before generation, and that targeted intervention can suppress it. DECOY provides certified ground truth and paired-tested baselines for evaluating hidden-state monitors.

title_en: Architectures and KV Replay for Depth-Recurrent Language Models
abstract_en: Depth recurrence increases effective model depth by repeatedly applying a fixed computation block. However, sharing attention parameters does not share the key-value (KV) states generated at different recurrence iterations, which causes memory growth with recurrence depth during autoregressive decoding. We study how to reduce this memory cost through architectural and cache-sharing approaches within a common depth-recurrent framework. We first study a looped hybrid that repeats a stack of Transformer layers, with recurrent mLSTM or Gated DeltaNet blocks replacing most attention layers and periodic Transformer attention anchors retained. We then restrict recurrence to a dedicated recurrent workspace in a Parcae-style architecture and test its stabilising adapter as a wrapper for the looped hybrid. Finally, we train a looped Transformer with recurrent KV replay, where only selected recurrence iterations write KV states that later iterations reuse. This trains the model to operate with the same shared KV topology used during inference. We find that looped hybrids require sufficiently frequent attention anchors, with performance depending strongly on the recurrent mixer. For cross-iteration KV sharing, recurrent KV replay allows multiple recurrence iterations to reuse the same KV states while retaining performance close to the full looped Transformer with separate KV caches for each iteration.

title_en: Leakage-aware calibrated decision-level fusion for mental-health text classification
abstract_en: Decision-level fusion benefits from complementary errors, calibrated probabilities, and leakage-aware evaluation. We evaluated a heterogeneous transformer fusion framework on 262,276 proxy-labeled Reddit records covering anxiety, depression, schizophrenia, and suicidal ideation. In a stratified random split, MinHash-LSH identified 29.1% of test records as lexical near-duplicates of training data. Augmentation-lineage auditing found 50.2% lineage overlap with training, including 30.0% of records retained after lexical filtering. We therefore used lineage-disjoint partitions. Twelve encoders, comprising three seeds each of Bio-ClinicalBERT, MentalBERT, MentalRoBERTa, and RoBERTa-base, underwent cross-fitted validation for calibration and ensemble selection. A class-specific Complementarity Index (CI), defined as the Jaccard distance between members' correctly classified validation sets, was assessed against independent fusion gain. CI correlated with gain for depression (r=0.50) and suicidal ideation (r=0.68), but not anxiety; results for schizophrenia were mixed. The selected MentalBERT, MentalRoBERTa, and RoBERTa-base triad achieved macro-F1 0.844 [0.823, 0.863], MCC 0.779, and ECE 0.0033 after post-fusion recalibration, improving macro-F1 by 0.021 [0.007, 0.037] over the validation-selected best single encoder. Integrated-Gradients attribution diversity was 2.3 times greater in fusion-rescued cases. Removing divergence-driving words destroyed 58% of rescues, versus 12% under random removal. These findings show that lineage auditing detects dependencies missed by lexical filtering, while class-specific complementarity and post-fusion calibration reveal ensemble behavior obscured by aggregate accuracy.

title_en: A Comparative Evaluation of BERT-Based and LLM-Based Models for Indic Sentence Similarity
abstract_en: The relative effectiveness of BERT-based encoders and large language model (LLM)-based embeddings for Indic semantic textual similarity remains insufficiently characterized. title_en: Does a completed simulation run mean a usable urban wind result for AI agents?
abstract_en: AI agents based on large language models (LLMs) can now configure and run computational fluid dynamics (CFD) solvers, but a completed run does not ensure that delivered metrics can be recomputed from raw outputs. This gap was examined for urban wind simulation, where multi-case comparisons must hold non-target conditions fixed and reported values must be traceable to raw samples. UrbanWind-AgentBench, comprising 200 tasks and 367 cases in 10 engineering task families, was constructed. Public task contracts specify variable factors, fixed conditions, numerical thresholds and deliverable requirements, and two-layer scoring separates a structural score for deliverables, run provenance and raw evidence from a numerical score obtained by independent recomputation against references. WindPilot was then proposed as an execution framework that incorporates contract parsing, execution provenance, deterministic verification and bounded acceptance review into the LLM execution loop. On 30 OpenFOAM tasks with independent references, at least the structural maximum of 60 points was reached by a base agent on 28 tasks, but numerical credit was obtained on only 6. With the same model name and budget, WindPilot increased the number of tasks with numerical credit to 17, full-score tasks from 0 to 3 and the mean task score from 62.5 to 72.5. Mean action steps fell from 130.4 to 104.9, and mean token consumption decreased by 12.9%. The mean gain for atmospheric boundary layer (ABL) tasks was 18.5 points. A completed simulation run is therefore not sufficient for a usable urban wind result; usability depends on checks that tie reported metrics to raw evidence during execution.

title_en: One Run Is Not Enough: Reminding a small Gemma 4 coding agent of its last finding made no measurable difference in a paired test
abstract_en: When a coding agent runs out of room, its earlier findings are cut and it forgets them. We tested a simple fix: automatically putting the agent's last finding back in front of it.
